title: Electricity
detail: A single hyperscale data center draws as much power as 80,000–400,000 homes. AI workloads require 5–10× more power per rack than traditional cloud computing. This demand is straining regional grids and driving rate increases for all ratepayers.
source: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2024 Data Center Energy Report

title: Water
detail: Evaporative cooling — the most common type — consumes 1–5 million gallons of water per day per large facility. In water-stressed regions like Arizona and Texas, this represents a significant draw on municipal and aquifer supplies.
source: Pacific Institute, Water Use in Data Centers, 2023

title: Noise
detail: Cooling equipment and diesel backup generators produce continuous noise at 65–85 dB at the property line — comparable to heavy traffic or a lawn mower. Noise attenuates with distance but rarely falls below 45 dB within 500 feet.
source: EPA Noise Standards; industry acoustic studies, 2022–2024

title: Air Quality
detail: Large facilities require 20–100 diesel backup generators for power redundancy. During testing (required monthly) and outages, these emit NOx, PM2.5, and CO. Facilities in environmental justice communities face disproportionate impact.
source: EPA RICE NESHAP regulations; community air monitoring studies

title: Tax Abatements
detail: Developers routinely negotiate Payment in Lieu of Taxes (PILOT) agreements that reduce or eliminate property taxes for 10–20 years. A 200 MW facility may receive $200–500M in foregone tax revenue — costs borne by other taxpayers and school districts.
source: Good Jobs First, Subsidy Tracker; state economic development records

title: Property Values
detail: The evidence is thinner than either side admits. An Indiana analysis found home values near data centers grew more slowly than the surrounding county at 3 of 4 sites; a George Mason study of Northern Virginia found no town-wide decline. The credible concern is adjacency — noise, lighting, traffic, and transmission lines hitting the closest homes.
source: Integra Realty Resources Indiana analysis (via WVPE, 2026); George Mason University Schar School, 2025
